newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD - U.S. rates the only show in town.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - U.S. rates the only show in town.

text.p: There will be one preoccupation for financial markets this week -- U.S. interest rates.
A meeting by the Federal Reserve's policy-setting committee will overshadow other events, though French data and an Italian mini-budget will spark interest in Europe, analysts said.

"The key question is which way the market is going to jump," said David Hewitt, bond strategist at Tokyo Mitsubishi International. "(A rise) is priced in but historically the markets have struggled when the Fed has tightened even though it's well anticipated."
The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meets on Tuesday amid increasing speculation interest rates will be put up.
Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan upped the anticipation for a rise in Congressional testimony last Thursday after stressing the importance of pre-emptive action to stifle inflation.

A Reuters poll of 48 economists showed that 34 expect the Fed to raise the key federal funds rate to at least 5.50 percent from 5.25 percent, up from 17 out of 44 who made the projection in the previous survey.
The U.S. Treasury yield curve flattened significantly last Thursday, reflecting market expectations of a rate rise at the short end and confidence of inflation vigilance at the long end.
Also on Tuesday, a two-year U.S. note auction is taking place, in a week of heavy government debt issues, analysts said.

"The two year auction is interestingly enough going to be on the Tuesday as well," Adam Chester, international bond strategist at Yamaichi International in Europe said. "Bidding will go in before the FOMC announcement."
The U.S. also auctions five-year notes on Wednesday while Japan was expected to announce a two-year and 10-year note sale next week. Britain sells 2.5 billion stg of 10-year notes on Wednesday.

U.S. data releases include March consumer confidence on Tuesday and February durable goods orders on Wednesday. In Europe, France has a full set of numbers but pickings will be slim elsewhere as markets edge into the Easter holiday.
France releases February consumer prices and housing starts on Tuesday, January industrial production on Thursday and February unemployment data on Friday.

"We expect industrial production for January and housing and consumption data for February to show increases and some green shoots coming through," Gwyn Hacche, senior European economist at James Capel in London, said.

"That should also be confirmed by the French industrial trends survey on Thursday but we think French unemployment will continue edging up by 10,000 in February," he said, echoing market consensus and forecasts for an unemployment rate of 12.7 percent, steady on January's figure.
"We still think it has a little bit further to go before it peaks," he added.
Italy's mini-budget will also be of interest, analysts said.
Cabinet secretary Enrico Micheli said on Friday the government would unveil a mini-budget before the end of the month which would include 15-16 trillion lire of deficit cutting measures.

"The question is what is the quality of budget reducing measures? Are they accounting adjustments or one-off measures?," Hacche said. "I think people are expecting quite a large bit of the 15 trillion to be of that sort rather than sustainable reductions."
March west German cost of living data arrives this week. A poll of economists by Reuters expects no change on the 1.7 percent year-on-year rise registered in January.

"The main focus will be the U.S. of course," Hacche said. "We are saying he will keep rates on hold on the argument he will be looking through the recent strength towards a slowing economy at the end of the year," he said.
